title: Eaton Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Eaton wells have a 50 ft median depth, with finished well costs commonly modeled at $7,800-$14,800.
h1: What Eaton, Colorado Well Records Tell Buyers
intro_html:
Eaton sits on the Weld County plains, where nearby well records commonly show shallow water and strong reported yields. The data covers permitted wells within 5 miles of Eaton and includes 1,738 Colorado DWR records. That does not mean every lot will perform the same. A permit record describes a nearby well, not a guarantee for your parcel.

For a buyer, the useful starting points are depth, water level, construction history, and the purpose of the well. Eaton's records include domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells. Before closing or planning a home, match the surrounding records to the exact property, confirm the legal water use, and have a driller evaluate access, geology, casing, grout, pump sizing, and septic layout.

sections.heading: Eaton wells are usually shallow, but the outliers matter
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Eaton is 50 feet, with the middle half between 32 and 70 feet. That is a favorable starting point for a drilling estimate in this plains setting. A driller bidding a typical residential well may be working in shallow alluvium or plains sedimentary material, but should still carry an allowance for variation.

Depth is not uniform across the area. Eighty-six percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 7% fall between 100 and 300 feet and another 7% between 300 and 600 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 220 feet, and the deepest record reaches 3,340 feet. Those extremes are why nearby logs and the exact lot matter more than a countywide assumption.

sections.heading: Reported Eaton yields are strong, with an important qualification
sections.html:
Among the 276 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 236.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 15.0 to 600.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-nine percent of those reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute, 20% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 2% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures are encouraging, but they are not a household guarantee. The yield sample is much smaller than the total permit record, and many wells are for irrigation or other uses. A residential buyer should ask for the well construction report, pump test information, permitted use, and any limits on pumping. An exempt household-use well is still subject to Colorado rules, including the 35 gallon-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit.

sections.heading: Eaton's water levels are shallow in the available records
sections.html:
Only 120 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. Within that group, the median depth to water is 9 feet, and the middle half is 7 to 28 feet. That suggests shallow groundwater is common in the records, which can reduce lift requirements but can also make construction and septic planning more sensitive to seasonal or local conditions.

The permit data provided here does not include a water-level series by decade, so it does not establish a dropping or rising long-term water table. Do not treat a shallow static level as a guaranteed well yield. Static level, pumping drawdown, recharge, well storage, and pump performance are separate questions. A driller can verify conditions through nearby logs and testing at the property.

sections.heading: Eaton's permit history includes active recent drilling
sections.html:
Eaton has a long permit record rather than a brief burst of development. Permits issued by decade include 173 in the 1950s, 182 in the 1960s, 105 in the 1970s, 98 in the 1980s, 170 in the 1990s, 190 in the 2000s, 193 in the 2010s, and 211 in the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2025.

The most active named drillers are Lesh Drilling Inc. (Lesh Jr., Ed), with 247 records; Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 202; and Clement, Glenn A., with 68. These names show who appears most often in the records, not who is available or best for your lot today. Confirm licensing, insurance, references, current scheduling, and the scope of each proposal before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new Eaton well may cost
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $35 to $55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At Eaton's 50-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $1,800 to $2,800. That is only the borehole portion, not a finished water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $7,800 to $14,800. A quote can move outside that range because of access, casing and grout requirements, difficult material, pump capacity, trench length, electrical service, water testing, or a deeper-than-expected hole. Ask the contractor to separate drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit-related work so bids can be compared directly.

sections.heading: Eaton buyers should check water quality, use, and septic fit
sections.html:
The mapped environmental inventory deserves attention. Within about 10 miles, the records show 960 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine feature, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not prove a particular well is contaminated, but it is a strong reason to test existing water and obtain site-specific guidance before relying on a well.

Most named aquifers are unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 1,393 wells; 187 are listed as Alluvial and 31 as Quaternary Alluvium. No Denver Basin aquifer wells are recorded. Use mix also matters: 41% irrigation, 29% domestic or household, 20% monitoring, and 11% stock. Confirm that the permit allows the use you need. Keep the well, septic system, replacement area, drive, and house site coordinated, and evaluate low-yield or dry-hole risk even when nearby records look favorable.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Eaton, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Eaton is 50 feet, and the middle half runs from 32 to 70 feet. Eighty-six percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet. Still, 7% are 100 to 300 feet and 7% are 300 to 600 feet, so a local driller should review nearby logs before giving a firm depth estimate.

faq.q: How much water do Eaton wells produce?
faq.a: Of the Eaton-area wells that report a pump yield, the median is 236.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 15.0 to 600.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-nine percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. These records include many irrigation wells, so a buyer should not assume the same result for a household well without a pump test and permit review.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Eaton?
faq.a: The local model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 50-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $1,800 to $2,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $7,800 to $14,800. Access, deeper drilling, casing, grout, pump size, trench length, and electrical conditions can change the final bid.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Eaton, Colorado?
faq.a: Well water safety is property-specific. The mapped area includes 960 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine feature, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those locations do not establish contamination at your address. Test the existing well or new source through an appropriate laboratory, review nearby site history, and maintain treatment if testing identifies a problem.

faq.q: Can I build a home on an Eaton property with a well?
faq.a: A buildable lot needs more than a nearby well record. Confirm the DWR permit and allowed use, then verify water quantity, water quality, well location, septic setbacks, replacement area, driveway access, and electrical service. Eaton records include domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells, so an existing well may not legally serve a new household without the correct authorization or water-rights review.
